name: Motion
description: Understanding what motion is and how we describe it

content.overview: Ever notice how you can tell, without even thinking about it, when something's moving? A car driving past, a ball rolling across the floor, you walking to school—your brain just gets it. But what IS motion, really? Turns out it's simple: something's in a different spot than it was a second ago. That tiny idea is the seed for basically all of mechanics. {{viz:anim-01}}
content.explanation:
Let's start easy. What's motion? Just this: something is in a different place than it used to be. That's genuinely it—no hidden catch.

But stick with me, because it gets fun. For motion to happen, you need three things:
- **Something that's moving** (an object—you, a car, a soccer ball)
- **A change in position** (it's somewhere new)
- **Time** (that change didn't happen instantly, it took a bit)

Here's the thing though—"it moved" isn't very useful by itself. Imagine texting a friend "I'm on my way!" versus "I'm 2 blocks away, walking, be there in 5 minutes." Which one actually tells them something? Same idea here. You can describe motion with more and more detail:
- "The car moved" (okay... but where? how far? how fast?)
- "The car moved 100 meters" (now we've got distance)
- "The car moved 100 meters north" (displacement—now we know the direction too)
- "The car moved 100 meters in 10 seconds" (and now we're talking speed!) {{viz:formula-01}}

Think about your own walk to school. You might zigzag around a corner, pass a shop, cross a street—that whole path you actually walked is your distance. But if someone asks "how far is school from your house?" they usually mean the straight-line hop, which is your displacement. Same trip, two different numbers, both true.

Honestly, motion is the thread that ties all of mechanics together. Speed, velocity, acceleration, forces—every single one of them starts from this one idea of something changing position over time. {{viz:diagram-02}}

Here's a fun twist to leave you with: **motion is relative**. Right now you might feel like you're sitting perfectly still reading this. But Earth is spinning under you, and hurtling around the sun while it's at it. So are you "still" or "moving"? Both, depending on what you're comparing yourself to! A car cruising at 100 km/h on the highway is definitely moving relative to the road—but relative to you in the passenger seat, it feels like you're not going anywhere at all. Both are correct. Motion only makes sense once you ask "moving compared to what?"
keyPoints: Motion just means a change in position over time—nothing fancier than that
You need three ingredients: an object, a position change, and time
Distance, displacement, speed, and velocity are just different ways to describe that change in more detail
Motion is relative—whether something's "moving" depends entirely on what you're comparing it to
This one idea is the foundation everything else in mechanics builds on
content.whyItMatters: Once you get motion, everything else clicks into place easier—speed, acceleration, forces, all of it. It's also just genuinely useful in real life: figuring out if you'll make it somewhere on time, judging how fast a car is coming, understanding why your phone's GPS can tell you "12 minutes away." It all traces back to this idea of something changing position over time.
